CausalChain: Fasting/Nutrient stress -> Increased adipose lipolysis -> Elevated free fatty acids in circulation -> Hepatic activation of PPARα (promotes FGF21 and fatty acid oxidation) and PPARβ/δ (enhances lipogenesis and PC (18:0/18:1) synthesis) -> Augmented secretion of FGF21 and PC (18:0/18:1) -> Delivery of these mediators to skeletal muscle -> PPARα-dependent upregulation of muscle fatty acid uptake and oxidation -> Reduced circulating triglycerides and improved systemic insulin sensitivity
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that precise, simultaneous activation of hepatic PPARα and PPARβ/δ using dual agonists and modern gene editing tools synergistically increases the secretion of both the hepatokine FGF21 and the phosphatidylcholine species PC (18:0/18:1). These secreted factors, when delivered to skeletal muscle, engage muscle PPARα to reprogram lipid metabolism by enhancing fatty acid uptake and oxidation. This metabolic reprogramming leads to a decrease in circulating triglyceride levels and improved insulin sensitivity, as quantitatively confirmed through integrated lipidomic and transcriptomic analyses. The proposed liver-to-muscle communication pathway offers a novel therapeutic target for metabolic conditions such as NAFLD and insulin resistance.
Abstract: We propose that, in response to fasting and nutrient stress, simultaneous activation of hepatic PPARα and PPARβ/δ—via cutting-edge dual agonist therapies and gene modulation techniques—synergistically elevates the production of both FGF21 and a specific phosphatidylcholine species, PC (18:0/18:1). This dual secretory output is hypothesized to mediate a liver-to-muscle endocrine communication axis that reprograms skeletal muscle lipid metabolism through a PPARα-dependent pathway. Advanced lipidomic and transcriptomic technologies allow us to quantitatively characterize this mechanistic cascade, leading to enhanced fatty acid oxidation in muscle, reduced circulating triglycerides, and improved systemic insulin sensitivity. This integrated model refines existing paradigms and identifies a novel, actionable therapeutic target for systemic metabolic disorders such as NAFLD and insulin resistance.
Orignal_vs_New: The new hypothesis retains the essential causal steps of the original model—beginning with fasting/nutrient stress leading to adipose lipolysis, free fatty acid elevation, hepatic activation of PPARα and PPARβ/δ, and ending with improved muscle metabolism and systemic insulin sensitivity. However, it integrates contemporary technological capabilities such as dual agonist therapy, gene editing, and state-of-the-art lipidomic and transcriptomic profiling to enhance mechanistic clarity and quantifiability. Additionally, the revised hypothesis provides explicit details on how PC (18:0/18:1) works in tandem with FGF21 to activate muscle PPARα-dependent pathways, thereby bridging previously unaddressed gaps in the original causal chain and improving its practical testability.
